terms.raspberry-pi-5: The Raspberry Pi 5 is a small ARM-based computer that can run a full Linux operating system. Here, the 8 GB model is the physical host for storage, media, monitoring and personal applications. Its low power use and compact size are useful, while its CPU, memory and single-disk setup remain real constraints.
terms.ssd: An SSD stores data on flash memory with no moving parts. I use the 1 TB drive for the Pi's operating system, container data, databases and media because it handles frequent reads and writes better than the usual microSD card. It is fast and simple, but one drive is still one point of failure.
terms.ram: RAM is the fast working memory used by running applications. The Pi has 8 GB shared across the operating system and all 48 containers, so lightweight services and careful resource use matter. Data in RAM is temporary; persistent application state must still be written to the SSD or a database.
terms.debian: Debian is the Linux distribution installed as the Pi's operating system. It provides the host environment, package management and Linux kernel underneath Docker. Applications can then run either directly on Debian or inside isolated Compose projects.
terms.storage-throughput-endurance: Throughput describes how much data a drive can read or write over time, while endurance describes how much repeated writing it can tolerate. Containers, databases and logs exercise both. The SSD gives this Pi more comfortable sustained performance and a better fit for frequent writes than a microSD card.
terms.self-hosting: Self-hosting means running a service on hardware I control instead of depending entirely on a provider's servers. In this article, the Raspberry Pi takes over jobs such as file storage, photo management and media streaming. I gain control and flexibility, but I also become responsible for updates, security, storage and recovery.
terms.docker-containers: A Docker container packages an application with the libraries and settings it needs while sharing the Pi's Linux kernel. Here, containers let many unrelated services run on one small machine without installing every dependency directly on the host. The count is high because larger applications often include separate databases, caches and workers.
terms.dns: DNS is the system that translates names such as a website address into network locations. The Pi can act as the DNS resolver for devices at home and refuse requests for known advertising or tracking domains. That blocks many ads before a browser or app connects to them.
terms.ai-agent: An AI agent is software that can interpret a goal and take a sequence of actions, rather than only returning a text answer. In AI ToolHub, the agent can create files, run development commands and deploy a small tool to the Pi, giving me a way to build and publish utilities while away from my desk.
terms.arm-cpu: ARM is the processor architecture used by the Raspberry Pi 5. Its four CPU cores can work on several tasks at once, but they still have much less headroom than a large desktop or server. That constraint shapes decisions such as using lightweight containers and preparing media before playback instead of converting several videos live.
terms.nas: NAS stands for network-attached storage: folders kept on one machine and shared with other devices over the network. The Pi acts as a small NAS by exposing selected SSD directories to laptops and other clients. It centralizes files without requiring me to carry a USB drive between devices.
terms.microsd-card: A microSD card is the tiny flash-storage card commonly used to boot a Raspberry Pi. It is convenient, but databases, container writes and frequent logs can be a demanding workload for it. I use the SSD for the operating system and active data to get better sustained performance and endurance.
terms.docker-layers: Docker images are assembled from read-only filesystem layers, with a writable layer added when a container runs. Building, pulling and updating many images creates frequent storage activity. Keeping those layers on the SSD avoids putting this write-heavy workload on the Pi's microSD card.
terms.docker-compose: Docker Compose describes a group of containers and their networks, storage mounts, settings and startup relationships in a configuration file. I use a Compose project as the boundary for most applications, so each capability can be understood, updated and restarted as a unit.
terms.persistent-data: Persistent data is information that must survive a container being replaced or recreated, such as database records, configuration and uploaded files. I place it in deliberate directories or volumes instead of leaving it inside a container's temporary writable layer. That makes upgrades and recovery less mysterious.
terms.lan: LAN means local area network: the private network inside the home that connects the Pi, laptops, phones and TVs. Services reached only over the LAN are not automatically available from the public internet. This is the simplest and safest access boundary in the setup.
terms.tailscale: Tailscale creates a private encrypted network between approved devices, even when they are on different internet connections. It lets my own phone or laptop reach the Pi away from home as if they were on the local network, without opening a separate router port for every service.
terms.samba: Samba is software that lets Linux provide Windows-compatible network file shares. On this Pi, it exposes selected SSD folders so laptops can browse and edit them like attached storage. Its permissions also let different services receive only the access they need.
terms.smb: SMB is the network protocol used for shared folders and files by Windows, macOS and many Linux clients. Samba implements SMB on the Pi. It carries requests such as listing a directory, opening a document or saving a file across the home network.
terms.network-shares: A network share is a folder made available to other devices over the network. Samba exposes selected SSD directories as shares, so a laptop can open and save files without the disk being physically attached. Each share can have different access rules.
terms.read-only-mount: A read-only mount lets a container see files but prevents it from changing or deleting them. I use that boundary when a service only needs to inspect a directory. It limits the damage a mistake or compromised process could cause to the original data.
terms.filesystem-permissions: Filesystem permissions and ownership decide which users and processes may read, write or execute a file. Containers still encounter these Linux rules when host directories are mounted into them. Correct ownership fixes access problems without giving every service unnecessarily broad control.
terms.immich: Immich is the self-hosted photo and video library running on the Pi. Its app uploads photos, while the server provides albums, search and a web interface. The deployment also needs PostgreSQL, Valkey and a machine-learning service, so its files and application state require different backup plans.
terms.postgresql: PostgreSQL is the database Immich uses for structured information such as photo metadata, albums and application state. The original image files live separately, which is why protecting only the database or only the photo directory would produce an incomplete backup.
terms.valkey: Valkey is an in-memory data store used here by Immich for temporary state, caching and coordinating background jobs. It helps different parts of the application work together quickly, while PostgreSQL and the photo files remain the durable sources of important data.
terms.machine-learning-service: Immich runs a separate machine-learning service for features such as recognizing visual similarity and enabling image search. Keeping it as its own service lets that specialized workload run alongside the main application, database and job system, which is one reason a single visible app can require several containers.
terms.raid: RAID combines multiple disks to improve availability when a drive fails. The planned mirrored pool would keep a second copy of each disk block on another drive, but it would repeat accidental deletion or corruption too. That is why the article treats RAID and a separate backup as different protections.
terms.hdd-pool: An HDD pool groups multiple spinning hard drives into one storage system. I plan to move bulk photo and media data to a larger dedicated pool, likely using mirrored disks. That would add capacity and tolerate a drive failure, but it would still need a separate backup.
terms.backup: A backup is an independent copy designed to recover data after deletion, corruption, device loss or another failure. It should not depend on the same physical disk as the original. In this setup, RAID may improve availability, but the separate backup is what protects against a wider set of losses.
terms.jellyfin: Jellyfin is the self-hosted media server that scans the library and streams it to browsers, phones and TVs. It can send a compatible file unchanged or transcode it for a client. On the Pi, avoiding unnecessary live transcoding keeps CPU demand manageable.
terms.container-mount: A container mount makes a host directory or managed volume visible at a chosen path inside a container. Jellyfin receives the media directory this way, without owning the original files. Mount permissions can limit it to only the directories and access level it actually needs.
terms.transcoding: Transcoding converts media from one video or audio format into another while it is being served. Jellyfin does this when a client cannot play the original file directly. Live conversion is CPU-intensive on the Pi, so I prepare compatible versions beforehand when possible.
terms.direct-play: Direct play means Jellyfin sends the original media file without converting it. The client decodes the file itself, leaving the Pi to handle mostly storage and network work. That is far cheaper than live transcoding and allows the small machine to serve several compatible streams more comfortably.
terms.linux-kernel: The Linux kernel is the core of the operating system that manages the CPU, memory, devices and processes. Docker containers isolate applications but share the host's kernel instead of running a complete guest operating system each. That lower overhead makes containers practical on an 8 GB Raspberry Pi.
terms.health-checks: A health check is an automated test that asks whether a service is actually ready or functioning, not merely whether its process exists. Compose can use these checks to report unhealthy containers and delay dependent services until the backend they need is ready.
terms.media-automation-stack: Radarr and Sonarr manage movie and series workflows, Prowlarr coordinates search sources, and Bazarr handles subtitles. Together they reduce manual library work around Jellyfin. I later placed my own MovieHub request and approval flow in front of this stack.
terms.frontend-backend: The frontend is the browser interface a person interacts with; the backend handles application rules, storage and privileged operations. AI ToolHub separates these responsibilities into different containers, with MongoDB and the Codex runtime supporting the backend behind the scenes.
terms.mongodb: MongoDB is the document database used by AI ToolHub. It stores structured application records in flexible JSON-like documents. In this architecture it is a supporting service behind the frontend and backend, not a database that readers connect to directly.
terms.codex-runtime: The Codex runtime is the environment where the AI agent can inspect files, edit code and run development commands. AI ToolHub puts a web interface around that capability, allowing the agent to build and deploy small tools on the Pi rather than only discussing how they could be built.
terms.pi-hole: Pi-hole is a DNS-level filtering service. Devices ask it where internet names are located, and it can block requests to known advertising or tracking domains before those connections are made. That gives the home network one shared filtering point.
terms.monitoring-stack: This monitoring stack covers different views of the same Pi: Netdata and Beszel show resource use, Gatus checks endpoints, Prometheus stores metrics, Grafana visualizes them, and Dozzle helps inspect container logs. Together they make failures and slowdowns easier to connect to an actual cause.
terms.observability: Observability means collecting enough signals—such as metrics, logs and health checks—to understand what a running system is doing. On this Pi, it turns a vague report that something is slow into evidence about CPU, memory, disk, network or a particular container.
terms.public-internet: A service on the public internet can receive connections from outside the home network. That convenience also exposes it to automated scanning and attacks, so a healthy container is not automatically ready for public access. The article uses a VPS, encrypted tunnel and authentication boundary for selected services.
terms.application-aware-backups: An application-aware backup captures data in a state the application can restore consistently. Simply copying database files while they are changing can produce an unusable result. Databases usually need their own dump or snapshot procedure, while media files and configuration may use different backup methods.
terms.replication: Replication keeps additional copies of data synchronized on another disk or system, often to improve availability. Because changes and deletions may also be replicated, it does not replace a versioned, independent backup. The article separates these tools because each protects against different failures.
terms.router-port-forwarding: Router port forwarding sends traffic arriving at a public internet port to a device inside the home network. Opening many ports would expose individual Pi services directly and create more entry points to maintain. Tailscale avoids that for my personal access by using a private device network.
terms.cloudflare-tunnel: Cloudflare Tunnel lets a private service make an outbound connection to Cloudflare so visitors can reach it without a conventional inbound router port. I considered it for public access, but photo and media traffic brought trade-offs that led me to a VPS and WireGuard design instead.
terms.vps: A VPS is a virtual private server rented in a data centre with a public internet address. Mine acts as the public front door while the Raspberry Pi remains at home. Requests arrive at the VPS and travel to the Pi through an encrypted tunnel.
terms.caddy: Caddy is the web server and reverse proxy running on the public VPS. It accepts browser requests, handles secure web connections and forwards approved traffic through the tunnel to the correct service on the Pi. This gives the setup one controlled public entry point.
terms.wireguard: WireGuard is a lightweight protocol for creating an encrypted network tunnel. Here it connects the public VPS to the Raspberry Pi at home, so forwarded requests can cross the internet without exposing the Pi's internal service traffic in plain text.
terms.cloudflare-dns: Cloudflare DNS publishes the records that map the site's domain names to the public VPS. It tells a visitor's device where to begin the connection; Caddy, WireGuard and the authentication gateway then handle what happens after the request arrives.
terms.authentication-gateway: An authentication gateway checks a user's identity and access before a request reaches a protected application. Placing that decision at the shared entry point gives different self-hosted tools a consistent login boundary, rather than trusting every application to implement public access safely on its own.
